name: Erik Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's pruning season, so I'm out in the rows by half seven with the loppers and a flask of tea. We've got eleven hectares of apples and pears behind the house on Mill Lane, mostly Bramleys, Coxes and Conference, plus a few sheep that keep the grass down between the trees. My wife Ingrid does the books and works three days at the school office. What I love is the quiet in the orchard in February; what wears me out is September, when the pickers arrive and I'm running about with bins and a clipboard for six weeks straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How many pickers, and where do they come from?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About fourteen at the peak, some from the village and some who come back year after year from abroad. Teodor has been coming for nine seasons, he knows the Conference rows better than my own son does. I pay them by the bin, and I'm proud that nobody's ever left my farm short-changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it stay a tool. I've no use for it myself, I've never even asked one of those chat programs a question. Down at the growers' meeting I'd say we've got bigger problems, like the price the packhouse pays us for Bramleys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much for me. My trees don't care what's on a computer. The only thing I'd watch is whether the supermarkets use it to squeeze us even harder on price, because they'll use anything for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal, really. I'd replace the old sprayer I've been patching, which I'd planned anyway, about nine thousand for a second-hand one. Maybe Ingrid would use it for the paperwork, that's her business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, if anything, that something on the news turned out to be less than the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the supermarkets will use anything to squeeze you. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago they rejected a whole load of Coxes because the skins had a bit of russet, that's a rough brown patch, and it's only looks. We had to sell them for juice at a fifth of the price. Nobody tasted them. It's always been about a computer-perfect apple, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ingrid use any of these tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's tried one for writing letters to the bank, I think. I told her I'd rather she wrote them herself, but she says it saves her an evening. We had a bit of a row about it, to be honest, and then I let it go.

S0.say: Let it stay a tool; I've never asked one of those chat programs a question. Growers have bigger problems, like the price the packhouse pays for Bramleys.
S0.think: It means very little for me, because my trees don't care what's on a computer. My only worry is the supermarkets using it to squeeze growers even harder on price.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and replaces the patched-up sprayer with a second-hand one for about nine thousand, as already planned. Leaves the paperwork tools to Ingrid.
S0.feel: Fine, and a bit relieved that the fuss came to less than the news said.
S0.quote: Nobody tasted them. It's always been about a computer-perfect apple, AI or not.
S0.fieldNote: He was relaxed but went straight to the supermarkets, which seem to be his villain in every story. The rejected Coxes clearly still rankle. The small row with his wife over her writing tool hints at how firmly he keeps technology at arm's length.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, with rules, so the companies can't just run off with it. If firms are hiring fewer young people, the government should be stepping in with apprenticeships. I'd say that at the growers' meeting and probably get a few eye rolls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow suits me. I'll be in my fifties by then and can keep doing it my way. What bothers me is the hiring fewer beginners bit, because my son Leo is fifteen and that's his first job gone before he gets there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe two hundred, into Leo and Ella's savings. I'd push Leo to get a trade, electrician or something, rather than an office job. On the farm I wouldn't change a thing; the trees take seven years to come good, so I'm not ripping them out for a fad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, but a knot in my stomach for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Leo about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, learn something you can do with your hands that a computer can't. Then I'd probably hear myself and think, that's what my dad said to me, and look where it got me. A mortgage and frost on the blossom. But he'd still be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any task on the farm you'd be glad to see disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spray records, maybe. Every time I spray I write down the product, the dose, the weather and the row, and it takes ages. If something did that on its own and I didn't have to touch it, fine. But I wouldn't go looking for it.

S1.say: Ten years is enough to bring in rules so companies can't run off with it. If firms hire fewer young people, the government should step in with apprenticeships.
S1.think: A slow change suits me, since I'll be in my fifties and can keep doing things my way. The worry is my son Leo losing his first job before he even gets there.
S1.do: Puts about two hundred a month extra into the children's savings and pushes Leo toward a trade like electrician. Changes nothing on the farm, since new trees take seven years to pay off.
S1.feel: Calm about himself, with a knot in his stomach about his children.
S1.quote: I'd probably hear myself and think, that's what my dad said to me, and look where it got me.
S1.fieldNote: His worry shifted entirely onto his son once beginners' jobs came up. He caught himself repeating his father's advice and laughed at it, but stood by it. He'd only accept new technology for chores like spray records if it came to him without effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let big tech run things without a union at the table. Office workers are getting what farm workers got thirty years ago when the machines came in. I'd sign the petition, I'd probably share something angry on the village page and then delete it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not my job going, it's Ingrid's. She works in the school office doing admin, and that's exactly the routine stuff they mean. Her wage is about a third of what keeps us afloat, so it's my problem too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit down with Ingrid and the mortgage letter and work out what we can drop. We've got about four months of savings, so I'd want her to look for something else before she's pushed, maybe at the farm shop in the next village. I'd also go and talk to the union rep at the growers' group, see if anyone's organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like it's coming in through the back door, through Ingrid, when I'd been watching the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Ingrid's wage went, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan on her Fiesta, we'd sell it and share mine. Then the kids' swimming. The orchard can't take a cut, you can't skip a frost spray because money's tight, the whole crop goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take one of those new AI jobs, if one appeared nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I wouldn't even know what it was. If they wanted someone to tell the computer what a good pear looks like, they'd have to come to me in the orchard, I'm not going to an office.

S2.say: This is what happens when big tech runs things without a union at the table. Office workers are getting what farm workers got when machines came in thirty years ago.
S2.think: It's not my job going, it's Ingrid's admin job at the school. Her wage is about a third of what keeps us afloat, so it hits me as well.
S2.do: Sits down with Ingrid and the mortgage letter, with about four months saved, and urges her to look for other work before she's pushed. Asks the union rep at the growers' group if anyone is organising.
S2.feel: Anxious, as if the change has come in through the back door through his wife.
S2.quote: It feels like it's coming in through the back door, through Ingrid, when I'd been watching the front.
S2.fieldNote: The threat arrived through his wife's job, which he hadn't expected and which made him visibly uneasy. Politically he reaches for unions and petitions, but personally he won't go near new AI jobs. He was clear the orchard costs can't be cut, so any savings come from the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, simple as that. If the people with shares and big houses are doing great while the doctor down the road and the lawyer in town are out of work, then tax it and spread it round. I'd go to the meeting in the town hall if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right, because nobody's going to replace me pruning a pear tree with a computer program. But the people who buy my fruit, the office workers, they're the ones losing jobs. If they can't afford local pears, they'll buy the cheapest imported ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fix our mortgage rate as long as the bank would let me, because if house prices are booming, rates won't stay put. I'd keep the sheep instead of selling them, a bit of insurance. And I'd go to Saturday market in town with our own juice and fruit, because I don't trust the packhouse price to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, odd as it sounds. Safe in the hands but worried about who's left to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your house would be worth a lot more in that picture. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper. It's not like I'm selling it, it's our home and the orchard's behind it. Ingrid's brother would say we're rich, but you can't eat a valuation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should get the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone who pays tax, and especially the ones who lost their jobs. The companies didn't build the roads or train the doctors. I know it's an old-fashioned left-wing thing to say, but I'd say it.

S3.say: The gains should be shared, simple as that. If people with shares are doing great while doctors and lawyers are out of work, tax it and spread it around.
S3.think: Nobody is replacing me pruning a pear tree with a computer program. But if the office workers who buy my fruit lose jobs, they'll buy the cheapest imported pears instead.
S3.do: Fixes the mortgage rate for as long as the bank allows and keeps the sheep as insurance. Starts selling his own juice and fruit at the Saturday market in town, so he isn't relying on the packhouse price.
S3.feel: Uneasy: safe in his own work but worried about who will be left to buy his fruit.
S3.quote: Nobody's going to replace me pruning a pear tree with a computer program. But the people who buy my fruit, the office workers, they're the ones losing jobs.
S3.fieldNote: He saw quickly that his safety is only as good as his customers' pay. His politics were plainest here: tax the gains and share them. The Saturday market idea was the one new thing he'd try, and even that is an old-fashioned way of selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ban them from picking until there are rules, full stop. I'd be at the protest with the pickers, Teodor and the lot. Online I'd say this isn't progress, it's just a few companies taking the last decent outdoor work there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done in five years, or near enough. A robot that picks and prunes doesn't need fourteen people every September, and the big orchards over the river will buy them first and undercut me. I can't afford one and I wouldn't know how to fix it when it broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd talk to Ingrid about whether we sell a few hectares to the neighbour while land's still worth something. I'd join any growers' group that's fighting for rules. And I'd stop planting new trees, which hurts to say, because a tree I plant now won't pay before the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. It's not the money only, it's being the last one who did it the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Teodor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that I'll keep him as long as I'm picking by hand, and I'd mean it. But he'd know, he's not daft. He'd probably tell me to buy a robot and let him drive it, and I'd say I'd rather sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd keep things as they are. Now you'd sell land. Which is closer to the truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I want to keep everything as it is, that's the honest wish. But if the price for pears drops because robot orchards are cheaper, wanting won't pay the mortgage.

S4.say: Ban robots from picking until there are rules. This isn't progress, it's a few companies taking the last decent outdoor work there is.
S4.think: I'm probably done in five years, because big orchards over the river will buy robots first and undercut me. I can't afford one and wouldn't know how to fix it.
S4.do: Talks with Ingrid about selling a few hectares to the neighbour while land still holds its value and joins growers fighting for rules. Stops planting new trees, since they wouldn't pay off before the robots arrive.
S4.feel: Alarmed and lying awake, as much about being the last one doing it the old way as about money.
S4.quote: A tree I plant now won't pay before the robots do.
S4.fieldNote: The calm of earlier scenarios disappeared completely. He was torn between a wish to keep everything the same and the knowledge that wanting won't pay the mortgage, and he admitted both when I named it. Loyalty to his long-time picker Teodor was what moved him most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, no question. What would help is rules on who can use them and how fast, and a fair price floor for fruit so small growers aren't undercut overnight. And money for older farmers to retire with dignity, not just a leaflet about retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pickers, really. Everyone talks about farmers, but it's the people like Teodor who'd lose the most. Make sure somebody asks them.

headlineQuote: A tree I plant now won't pay before the robots do.
portrait: Erik is a 43-year-old apple and pear grower on eleven hectares behind his house on Mill Lane, married to Ingrid, who works in a school office. He has never used an AI tool and doesn't want to, and he trusts unions, rules and fair prices far more than any new machine. Through the first four scenarios he feels safe in his own hands-on work but worries about his son's first job, his wife's admin job and the customers who buy his fruit. In the robot scenario his calm breaks: he'd stop planting trees, consider selling land and stand at the protest beside his pickers.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because big orchards would buy picking robots first and undercut a small grower who can't afford one.
whatWouldHelp: Rules on who can use robots and how fast, a fair price floor for fruit, and real money to let older farmers retire with dignity.
